body: The weekend flush has removed much of the leveraged long exposure that built up before the drop. That lowers the risk of another forced-selling cascade in the near term, but it does not bring in new buyers by itself. Sentiment is fragile. Several possible drivers are in play at once: ETF redemptions, rate-hike expectations and lingering exchange-security worries after the Binance hack. With that many headwinds, a recovery will need confirmation from flows rather than from price alone. Ether’s steeper loss keeps the ETH/BTC cross under pressure heading into the new week. Leveraged bulls paid for the weekend’s slide to a four-month low, and the bounce means little until ETF outflows stop. Bitcoin dropped to its lowest level since July over the weekend, trading as low as $62,000 before recovering to $64,910 by late Sunday afternoon US time, according to The Block’s price data. That still left the world’s largest cryptocurrency down 14.2% over the past seven days, and the selloff spread across the market to trigger roughly $2 billion in forced position closures. The damage was heavier further along the risk curve. Ether fell 18.2% over the week to $1,815, while Solana lost 19.7% to trade at $71.68, The Block reported. Ether underperforming bitcoin in a broad selloff is a familiar pattern, but a weaker ETH/BTC relationship on its own does not mean ether is cheap or due to catch up. CoinGlass hourly data showed crypto liquidations totalled $2.02 billion between 8 a.m. ET Saturday and 8 a.m. ET Sunday. Long positions accounted for $1.68 billion of that, against $342.4 million in shorts. A liquidation happens when an exchange closes a leveraged trade because the trader’s margin can no longer cover losses, and those forced sales can push prices lower and trigger the next round of liquidations. The roughly five-to-one skew toward longs shows that traders were leaning bullish with borrowed money going into the drop. By about 4:30 p.m. ET Sunday, the live 24-hour tally on CoinGlass had eased to $742.9 million as prices steadied. Binance co-founder and former CEO Changpeng Zhao used a post on X to deny rumours that the exchange had been selling crypto in the wake of its record hack on Oct. 29. Zhao said he had personally bought crypto over the past few days using stablecoins he recently received. He pointed to withdrawals from US spot bitcoin ETFs and expectations of another Federal Reserve rate hike as possible drivers of the slide, and suggested some investors may be raising cash for Anthropic’s planned IPO. He also cited lingering security concerns after the Binance hack. Those explanations are Zhao’s view rather than established causes. The ETF data does support part of that argument. US spot bitcoin ETFs recorded $1.91 billion in net outflows across seven straight trading sessions through Friday, The Block reported earlier. Spot ether ETFs lost $398.9 million last week, their seventh consecutive week of withdrawals and one short of the record run of eight. Outflows show reduced demand through these products, but they do not by themselves tell us who is selling or why. What to watch next: the first test is whether bitcoin can hold above the weekend low near $62,000 now that much of the leveraged long exposure has been cleared out. A halt to the ETF outflow streak, ideally confirmed over several completed sessions, would add evidence that product demand is stabilising. If spot ether ETFs post an eighth straight week of withdrawals, they would match their record. One calmer session after a liquidation flush is not proof of a bottom, so a practical approach is to watch both the flow trend and the price response before treating the recovery as durable. body: A flat quarter made weak mainly by trade is unlikely to derail BoJ tightening plans by itself. Strong capex and positive domestic demand are the parts policymakers watch most closely. The miss still gives the yen little help just as USD/JPY presses toward 160, and that raises the stakes for any comments from Japanese officials on the currency. JGB yields may ease slightly at the front end if traders trim December hike bets. The bigger driver for the session is Takata’s speech later today, where a hawkish response to the data would quickly restore conviction. For the Nikkei, softer growth and a weak yen are a familiar, broadly supportive mix for exporters. Japan’s Q3 stall was a trade story more than a domestic one: exports and cautious shoppers dragged, but strong business investment leaves the BoJ’s December hike case largely intact. Japan’s economy stalled in the July to September quarter. Preliminary data showed real GDP contracted at an annualised 0.1%, short of the 0.3% growth economists had expected and a sharp slowdown from 1.4% in the second quarter. On a quarterly basis, output was flat, against a forecast of a 0.1% gain. The miss came from two places. External demand subtracted 0.6 percentage point from growth, more than the 0.4 point drag expected, with exports slipping 0.2% from the previous quarter. Private consumption, which accounts for more than half of the economy, fell 0.3%, a slightly deeper drop than the 0.2% decline forecast. Business investment was the bright spot. Capital expenditure jumped 1.6% from the prior quarter, just ahead of expectations of 1.5%, and reversed a 0.9% fall in the April to June period. Overall, domestic demand added 0.6 percentage point to growth, which shows the weakness was concentrated in trade rather than in the domestic economy as a whole. Price pressure across the economy also came in a little softer. The GDP deflator, a broad measure of prices across the economy, rose 2.4% from a year earlier, below forecasts and the previous quarter’s 2.6%, though still comfortably above the Bank of Japan’s 2% target. The figures land at a sensitive moment for the BoJ, which held its policy rate at 1.25% in October and is widely expected to raise it to 1.5% in December. A flat quarter driven by trade, alongside firm capital spending and positive domestic demand, gives policymakers grounds to look through the headline number. The softer consumption reading, however, will give more cautious board members something to point to. Attention now turns to BoJ board member Hajime Takata, who speaks later on Monday at 04:00 GMT (11:00 pm ET Sunday). Takata has dissented at recent meetings in favour of faster tightening, and his read on the data will be watched for any shift in the December debate. A revised GDP estimate is due next month and could change the picture if the capex or consumption figures are updated. Your market education doesn't end here. title: Trump out of public view since Wednesday, fuelling speculation on his wherabouts
summary: For markets, this is a non-event as long as the official record keeps showing normal activity. Traders have learned to discount social media speculation about the president’s health, and nothing so far has moved oil, Treasuries or the US dollar on this story. The risk lies in his travel plans. A smooth departure for China would close the story, but an unexplained delay or cancellation would quickly become a factor for markets. body: For markets, this is a non-event as long as the official record keeps showing normal activity. Traders have learned to discount social media speculation about the president’s health, and nothing so far has moved oil, Treasuries or the US dollar on this story. The risk lies in his travel plans. A smooth departure for China would close the story, but an unexplained delay or cancellation would quickly become a factor for markets. With the Iran war still shaping energy prices , any real uncertainty at the top would tend to lift oil’s risk premium and support safe-haven demand for the dollar. Trump’s few days out of view have set off the usual online rumours, but the documented record shows a president working behind closed doors, and an expected trip to China this week should put him back in front of the cameras. President Donald Trump has not made a public appearance since Wednesday, a gap that has stirred online speculation about his whereabouts. However, the official record of his activity over that period points to a president working out of view rather than one who is absent. The most recent sighting came on Thursday, when Trump recorded a video interview with sports commentator Stephen A. Smith inside the White House. On Saturday the White House called a travel and photo lid, the routine notice that the president will not be seen publicly that day. On Sunday, his published schedule showed him working from early morning until late evening on calls and meetings, and Trump posted on Truth Social that he was at the White House holding meetings on a range of subjects. Calendar entries also record a Sunday visit to his golf club and his return. The low profile has drawn attention largely because it overlapped with Friday’s nationwide FAA ground stop, which Trump has not addressed in public. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy has linked that disruption to faulty work on a telecom systems upgrade at a remote site, and the response so far has been led by cabinet officials. Some social media accounts have gone further, suggesting without evidence that the president is unwell or worse. Nothing in the public record supports that. Scrutiny of the schedule has run well ahead of the evidence, and the documented calendar, posts and official accounts describe his movements rather than any change in his health. Short absences like this are not new. Trump went about a week without a public appearance in late May and early June before returning to announce an executive order from the Oval Office. In April, during a similar quiet spell in the Iran war, the White House said he was working nonstop. The next clear test is his travel this week. Trump is expected to go to China for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit, scheduled for November 18 and 19 in Shenzhen, which would put him back in front of cameras within days. body: A services reading at a multi-year high, led by new orders, strengthens the case that New Zealand’s recovery is spreading beyond a handful of sectors. That gives the New Zealand dollar modest support on the domestic data front. For rate expectations, firmer activity reduces the pressure for further policy support. The flat employment reading and persistent cost-of-living complaints, however, point to slack that has not yet closed. Traders are likely to treat the data as a confidence builder rather than a game changer, and will look to the next few releases to see whether spending held back during the election starts to come through. New Zealand’s services firms are finally seeing new business arrive in volume heading into summer, but with hiring still flat, October’s strength looks more like a pre-Christmas lift than a recovery that has fully taken hold. New Zealand’s services sector expanded for a fifth consecutive month in October, with the BNZ-BusinessNZ Performance of Services Index climbing to 51.7 from 50.9 in September. That is the strongest reading in more than three and a half years. A reading above 50 signals expansion. The gain was led by forward-looking measures. New orders and business rose to 53.0, activity and sales reached 52.6, and supplier deliveries came in at 52.1. Employment was the only sub-index in contraction, edging just below breakeven at 49.9, and stocks and inventories eased to 50.1. BusinessNZ chief executive Katherine Rich said the run of readings above breakeven stood out against the past few years. She said it was encouraging to see activity and new business rising together heading into summer. She suggested that many firms had put decisions on hold before the election, and that some of that delayed spending and investment could start to come through by the end of the year once a new government is formed. Survey comments showed businesses are still preoccupied by fuel prices, the cost of living, interest rates and election uncertainty. On the positive side, respondents pointed to the run-in to summer, Christmas bookings and the return of tourists. The share of negative comments fell to 57.9% from 59.9% in September, a modest improvement in tone. Economists said firmer services activity is especially welcome because of the sector’s weight in the New Zealand economy and its importance for the GDP outlook. If the improvement holds, they said, it would add to evidence that the recovery is broadening and becoming more established. The softness in hiring is the main caveat. Firms appear willing to take on new business but are not yet adding staff. The next few months will show whether the election delay was the main drag on investment and jobs, or whether the caution runs deeper. Your market education doesn't end here. title: Asia Is Building 73% of the World's New Nuclear Capacity
summary: The Middle East crisis and the spiking oil and gas prices have shifted the Asian nations’ priorities to energy security and generating electricity with homegrown resources. Renewable energy capacity is soaring, not only in the top emerging markets China and India, but also across Southeast Asia, as the Strait of Hormuz crisis hiked LNG prices and dented gas demand. Another clean energy source, nuclear capacity, is also gaining momentum globally. Countries worldwide started thinking about adding or building nuclear reactors for the first time…
body: What I Cover Tsvetana Paraskova is an energy and commodities journalist who has contributed to Oilprice.com for nearly a decade, covering global energy markets, commodities,… The Middle East crisis and the spiking oil and gas prices have shifted the Asian nations’ priorities to energy security and generating electricity with homegrown resources. Renewable energy capacity is soaring, not only in the top emerging markets China and India, but also across Southeast Asia, as the Strait of Hormuz crisis hiked LNG prices and dented gas demand. Another clean energy source, nuclear capacity, is also gaining momentum globally. Countries worldwide started thinking about adding or building nuclear reactors for the first time in the wake of the previous energy crisis in 2022-2023. Construction will take years, but rising nuclear capacity could combine with the renewables surge to change the long-term gas and coal demand patterns in Asia’s economies. The world currently has 408 gigawatts (GW) of total operating nuclear power capacity. Another 91 GW is under construction, according to the Global Energy Monitor’s Global Nuclear Power Tracker . Of the 91 GW of nuclear capacity in the construction stage, as much as 73%, or 66 GW, are in Asia, per the data compiled by Reuters columnist Gavin Maguire. Asia also leads in utility solar and wind power construction, as smaller emerging markets add to powerhouses China and India in boosting their renewable energy capacities. China and India still rely on coal for a large part of their electricity supply and continue to approve and build coal-fired power plants, but they are also betting big on nuclear and renewables to meet soaring electricity demand. Globally, China, India, Japan, and South Korea are the top four countries currently building the most nuclear power capacity in the world, according to the Global Energy Monitor (GEM) data. China leads with more than 43 GW under construction, followed by India with 6.6 GW, Japan with 6.1 GW, and South Korea with 5.6 GW. China, the world’s second-largest economy after the U.S., is not picking one electricity source over another—it is building more of everything to meet rising demand. China is a global leader in coal, renewables, and nuclear power additions and planned projects as its primary goal is energy security and fewer fossil fuel imports at low prices, preferably. India has also become a renewable energy powerhouse in recent years. India has also boosted battery and other energy storage to support the rapid expansion of solar PV capacity installations, but it needs much more to ensure the curtailment rates of renewable energy are reduced. The world’s most populous country, while still betting big on coal power capacity, has huge plans in the nuclear power sector, too. India’s goal is to boost its installed nuclear power capacity to 100 GW by 2047, up from just 8.8 GW now. At the end of 2025, India’s government approved the landmark Atomic Energy Bill, which allows private companies to invest in its nuclear energy industry for the first time, as the country looks to boost nuclear power capacity tenfold within two decades. Moreover, India expects to build five small modular reactors (SMRs) domestically by 2033, India’s Atomic Energy Minister, Jitendra Singh, said earlier this year. Developed Asian economies Japan and South Korea are also betting on nuclear power additions, which is especially telling of the energy security concerns since 2022. Japan has made a U-turn in nuclear energy policy and plans to rely more on nuclear reactors for its power supply in the coming decades. The country looks to have 20% of its electricity supply coming from nuclear power by 2040, up from below 10% now. Before the Fukushima meltdown in 2011, nuclear energy accounted for about 30% of Japan’s electricity mix. title: Oil prices steady as Middle East tensions persist - The Vibes
body: Brent holds near US$95.50 and WTI at US$88.50 a barrel as investors weigh renewed attacks in the Gulf against expectations of a global supply surplus CRUDE oil prices were largely unchanged on Monday as renewed hostilities in the Middle East kept supply concerns in focus, while expectations of an improving global supply balance limited further gains. West Texas Intermediate (WTI) crude traded around US$88.50 a barrel, while Brent crude hovered near US$95.50 after sharp price swings last week. Tensions escalated after Iran struck a US helicopter base in Bahrain on Sunday, marking its first attack on a Persian Gulf state in several weeks. Iranian state television also reported that five vessels had struck mines, while maritime authorities confirmed an attack on a tanker. All crew members were reported safe. However, hopes of a diplomatic resolution remained after Tehran indicated that negotiations were still possible, while US President Donald Trump said further strikes against Iran might not be necessary. Adding to the pressure on oil prices, the International Energy Agency (IEA) reported last week that global oil supply had exceeded demand for the first time since the conflict began. It projected a surplus of about two million barrels per day this quarter as shipments through the Strait of Hormuz gradually recover. On the currency front, the US Dollar Index (DXY), which measures the greenback against a basket of six major currencies, slipped 0.03 per cent to 103.379. The index has declined 1.37 per cent over the past four weeks but gained 3.81 per cent over the past 12 months. The US dollar also edged lower against the ringgit, with the USD/MYR exchange rate falling 0.04 per cent to 4.0845. Over the past four weeks, the pair has declined 0.05 per cent, while the ringgit has strengthened about 1.72 per cent against the US dollar over the past 12 months. Analysts' forecasts put the USD/MYR exchange rate at 4.07789 by the end of the current quarter and 4.01433 in one year. Hotter October inflation and a 6.5% producer-price surge put a December Fed hike fully on the table - Latin Times
body: The October consumer price index rose 0.4% from the month before, a tenth of a point above the 0.3% that economists had forecast. Food and shelter costs led the advance. Core CPI — which excludes food and energy — also registered 0.3%, matching its pace from each of the previous two months. The Bureau of Labor Statistics published the data on November 10. A monthly core reading around 0.2% would put annual inflation on course for the Fed's 2% target. Three consecutive months at 0.3% push the annualized three-month rate to 3.7%, the fastest clip of the year. The report carried an unusual footnote: federal statisticians were unable to publish an official 12-month CPI comparison because no price data were collected in October 2025, when a government shutdown halted the surveys. The Producer Price Index for October, released November 13, reinforced the picture. Wholesale prices rose 0.3% on the month and 6.5% on the year — the highest annual rate since November 2022, according to the BLS. Final-demand goods drove much of the increase, up 0.5%, while the services component edged 0.2% higher. Prices for truck transportation of freight surged 3.9%, accounting for more than 80% of the increase in final-demand services. Chicago Fed President Austan Goolsbee, in an interview on PBS NewsHour after the report, described the data as "borderline disturbing," warning that "we have got a real inflation issue on our hands that has been developing." Until recently, the internal Fed debate focused on the timing of rate cuts. That calculus flipped after the October numbers landed. Fed Governor Christopher Waller, speaking at a Bank of England conference in London on the day the CPI was released, said he would support a 25-basis-point increase at the December meeting. He added that if core inflation came in around 0.3% or higher, a 50-basis-point move should be considered as well. Dallas Fed President Lorie Logan was more direct: she said the FOMC needs at least two additional quarter-point hikes, followed by a pause to assess conditions. James McCann, senior economist for investment strategy at Edward Jones, told CBS News in an email that the October CPI report was the last look at inflation the Fed would get before its December meeting, adding that "it most likely seals the deal on a rate hike to close the year." Futures markets already reflect the shift. As of this writing, traders are fully pricing a quarter-point hike at the FOMC's December 8-9 meeting. The Fed's preferred inflation gauge — the Personal Consumption Expenditures price index — climbed from 3.4% in August to 3.6% in September. The Cleveland Fed's real-time model projects the PCE rate will reach 3.77% in October and 3.82% in November, extending the gap above the 2% target. The timing presents a procedural challenge. The November CPI report won't be published until December 10 — one day after the FOMC votes. Policymakers will have to decide without seeing the latest consumer-price reading. The reversal from expected cuts to probable hikes carries direct consequences. Mortgage rates, as measured by the Freddie Mac Primary Mortgage Survey , already stand near 7.18%. Consumer credit, auto loans, and business financing remain expensive or could become more so. For families that have already stretched budgets against years of elevated living costs , an additional tightening cycle is not a financial abstraction — it is tangible monthly pressure. Inflation has now run above the Fed's 2% target for more than five years. The data are on the table. The Federal Reserve's December meeting is three weeks away.

title: Economists expect SARB to hold interest rates steady despite rising inflation - thenational.co.za
body: Most economists expect the South African Reserve Bank (SARB) to keep interest rates unchanged when the Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) meets later this week, although a further 25-basis-point increase remains possible. Neil Roets, CEO of Debt Rescue, said the SARB faces a difficult decision, with inflation remaining above its target while consumers continue to struggle under the combined pressure of high living and borrowing costs. “Our expectation is that the Monetary Policy Committee will lean towards keeping interest rates unchanged, although a further 25-basis-point increase remains a possibility,” Roets said. He said inflation had increased to 4.5% in September from 4.4% in August, showing that price pressures remained a concern. However, recent declines in international oil prices offered some encouragement, although ongoing geopolitical tensions in the Middle East meant that sustained improvement was far from guaranteed. Roets said these developments strengthened the case for allowing previous interest rate decisions more time to work through the economy before further tightening was considered. The release of October’s Consumer Price Index (CPI) figures on 19 November, shortly before the MPC announcement, would also be important, he said. The data could provide further insight into whether previous monetary policy measures were beginning to produce the desired results. Roets added that many South African households had already absorbed years of rising living costs. Even when inflation slows, accumulated increases in essential expenses remain part of monthly budgets. “Declining international oil prices do not automatically translate into immediate reductions in fuel, transport or food costs,” he said. “A further interest rate increase would place additional pressure on households with variable-rate debt, particularly home loans and vehicle finance.” Johann Els, chief economist at PSG Financial Services, said that, on balance, the Reserve Bank was likely to leave interest rates unchanged. “Policy has done enough,” Els said. “There hasn’t been any serious second-round effect in inflation. The Reserve Bank has indicated that policy is restrictive, although there are still risks in terms of second-round effects.” Benay Sager, executive head of DebtBusters, also expects the interest rate to remain unchanged for now. “We do foresee a change in January, but it’s too difficult to say at the moment whether that will be an increase or decrease,” Sager said. The MPC would consider global macroeconomic factors as well as local indicators such as inflation, employment and fuel prices in making their decision, he said. “I think it will be particularly important to look at where the petrol price is expected to be,” Sager said. “That will be a main consideration.” Sager added that, although another increase was not expected, a rate hike would be challenging for consumers and could force many households to make difficult decisions about how they allocate their income. “Consumers will need to carefully consider their priorities and make sure they have enough money to service their debt,” he said. “If not, they should consider speaking to a debt counsellor.” Waldo Krugell, an economist at North-West University Business School, said the MPC might hold rates, particularly if lower oil prices and fuel-price relief continued to ease pressure on consumers. “But the rand may turn things on their head,” Krugell said. “I’m sticking with a hold for now, but we will have to see where the currency goes.” Professor Raymond Parsons, economist at the NWU Business School, said the MPC faced two options: raising interest rates again or pausing for now. “There are still upside risks to inflation, such as possible second-round effects,” Parsons said. “On the other hand, the fuel price outlook is more encouraging.” He said businesses and consumers should prepare for the possibility of higher borrowing costs. title: Capital Economics Warns AI Stock Decline Could Deepen as Earnings Forecasts Remain Elevated - Yahoo Finance
body: Capital Economics has warned that the recent decline in artificial intelligence-related stocks could continue, as analysts' earnings expectations for technology companies have yet to reflect growing concerns about the outlook for AI investment. In a research note published this week, the economic research firm highlighted a divergence between falling technology share prices and continued increases in corporate profit forecasts. "The AI correction in equities could have much further to run," Capital Economics wrote. The firm suggested that earnings estimates may eventually face downward revisions if investor sentiment continues to deteriorate or major technology companies begin reducing their planned expenditure on AI infrastructure. Capital Economics noted that analysts have continued raising profit expectations for companies benefiting from artificial intelligence investment, despite the recent weakness in their share prices. The firm attributed part of this divergence to the spending commitments made by hyperscalers, the large cloud computing companies responsible for substantial investment in AI infrastructure. Rather than reducing their expenditure plans, these businesses have continued to increase their commitments to computing capacity and related infrastructure. This spending has supported expectations for revenue and earnings growth among companies supplying AI processors, equipment and other technology. However, Capital Economics cautioned that analyst forecasts can take time to respond to changing market conditions. The firm believes current estimates may not fully reflect the possibility of weaker demand or a slowdown in AI-related investment. Capital expenditure by major cloud computing companies has been an important factor supporting the rise in AI-related technology shares. Capital Economics warned that any concrete indication of reduced spending commitments could lead investors to reassess expectations for companies benefiting from the AI investment cycle. A slowdown in hyperscaler expenditure could affect demand for semiconductors, data centre equipment and other infrastructure associated with artificial intelligence. The firm suggested that such developments could result in downward revisions to earnings forecasts that have continued to increase during the recent market decline. For now, hyperscalers have maintained or expanded their investment plans, but Capital Economics considers the potential for future reductions an important risk to monitor. European stock markets have performed comparatively well during the recent decline in AI-related equities. Capital Economics noted that the MSCI Europe Index recorded a modest gain last week, despite weakness in technology shares elsewhere. The firm acknowledged that a more substantial global equity sell-off could eventually affect European markets, as has occurred during previous periods of market stress. However, it suggested that the current situation may differ because the earlier AI-driven rally was concentrated in a relatively small group of technology companies. This concentration could mean that a further correction has a greater effect on markets with substantial exposure to AI-related stocks. "We expect Europe to continue to outperform if the bubble deflates further," Capital Economics said. The forecast reflects the firm's expectation of relative European market performance rather than an assumption that European equities would necessarily avoid losses. Capital Economics also expects the recent rally in US Treasury securities to continue if equity markets experience additional declines. The firm suggested that investors could increase their allocations to government bonds as they seek assets perceived as relatively safe during periods of market volatility. Increased demand for Treasuries generally supports bond prices and places downward pressure on yields. title: AI Data Center Stocks Crater On Nebius Outlook And Nvidia Uncertainty, But Applied Digital's (NASDAQ: APLD) $36.2B Lease Book Remains Intact - Foreign Policy Journal
body: A $36.2 billion portfolio of signed, non-cancellable leases did nothing to shield Applied Digital (NASDAQ: APLD) from a brutal morning session, as shares slid 10% despite zero company-specific news. The selloff swept across the AI infrastructure sector, with Nebius (NASDAQ: NBIS) dropping 13%, CoreWeave (NASDAQ: CRWV) losing roughly 10%, IREN (NASDAQ: IREN) shedding 10%, and Cipher Digital (NASDAQ: CIFR) falling 9%. The catalyst was Nebius, whose third-quarter revenue surged 571% to $980.8 million but included $325.1 million in non-recurring strategic partnership payments that raised quality-of-earnings questions. Bank of America flagged that Nebius’s guidance implies a sequential revenue decline in the fourth quarter, with delays at third-party data centers pushing recognized revenue into early 2027. A separate and arguably more alarming disclosure was a $40 billion capital spending plan for 2027, which rattled investors already sensitive to the pace of AI infrastructure buildout. Nvidia’s leadership transition compounded the anxiety, as The Information reported that the chipmaker is expected to pull back on AI investments and credit guarantees following Jensen Huang’s exit as CEO on Thursday. That report hit IREN particularly hard, given that Nvidia represents a $3.4 billion customer relationship for the company, while Cipher fell alongside news from the Wall Street Journal that private neocloud Nscale requires additional financing before its planned IPO. None of these developments altered a single dollar of Applied Digital’s contracted revenue, where two anchor tenants account for 86% of the total signed lease value: a tier-one hyperscaler holding $20.2 billion and CoreWeave holding $11 billion across 15-year agreements. CoreWeave’s own financial position draws scrutiny, with its bonds yielding above 17%, yet the leases carry no cancellation provisions and CoreWeave pays approximately 10% more per megawatt than hyperscaler peers. Wall Street expects Applied Digital’s revenue to more than triple between fiscal 2026 and fiscal 2028, with minimum lease payments alone projected to reach $1.58 billion in fiscal 2028, representing around 80% of that year’s consensus estimate. At today’s depressed price, Applied Digital trades at well under 5x forward sales, compared to a three-year average multiple of roughly 11x, a gap that suggests the market is pricing in risks beyond what the contracted backlog justifies. The genuine vulnerability is not the tenants but the capital required to bring additional capacity online: CEO Wes Cummins stated this month that the company must still finance approximately 800 MW over the coming 12 months. A sustained sector selloff raises the cost and complexity of that financing, meaning the fiscal second-quarter earnings report due in January becomes the sector’s next real stress test.
